params.text:
Making no assumptions

It is easy to make assumptions without realising it — to assume a woman has a husband, or that an older person could not possibly be gay, bisexual or trans. Assumptions like these can make a person feel invisible and unable to be open. Person-centred care means seeing each person as an individual and building support around their wishes, relationships and history — not around what you expect them to be. When you make no assumptions, people feel able to be themselves, which is the foundation of good care.

  • No default: do not assume anyone is heterosexual or that their gender matches their records.
  • Start with the person: ask what matters to them and how they wish to be supported, using open questions such as asking about “partners” rather than assuming a husband or wife.
  • Let people share at their pace: give people the space to be open, without pressure.
  • Record what they tell you: capture their preferences so care stays consistent across the team.
  • Keep an open, curious mind: be ready to learn about the person rather than filling in the gaps yourself.

Confidentiality about identity

A person’s sexual orientation and gender identity are private and sensitive information. If someone shares this with you, it is not yours to pass on. You should never disclose that a person is LGBTQ+ to their family, other people they know, or colleagues who have no need to know, without the person’s clear agreement.

Revealing someone’s identity without their consent is called “outing” them, and it can cause real harm — damaging relationships, or exposing someone to prejudice or danger. Only share such information with colleagues where it is genuinely necessary for the person’s care and where the person is content for you to do so.

A welcoming environment

People quickly sense whether a place is welcoming. Small, visible signals show LGBTQ+ people that they will be accepted. Inclusive-care guidance from organisations such as Stonewall, the NHS and Skills for Care encourages services to make inclusion visible and to use language that does not assume everyone is heterosexual.

  • Inclusive language: use words like “partner” on forms and in conversation.
  • Visible signals: welcoming imagery or symbols can quietly reassure people they are safe here.
  • A consistent culture: every member of the team helps set a respectful, accepting tone.

params.alt: A care worker sitting with an older person they support, beside the heading “Making no assumptions”. Key points: No default; Start with the person; Let people share at their pace.

params.question: A person you support tells you, in confidence, that she is a lesbian. Her daughter later asks you directly whether her mother has ever had a girlfriend. What should you do?

answers.text: Keep the information confidential and do not disclose her identity without her clear consent.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A person’s identity is private. Disclosing it without consent would be outing her, which can cause real harm.

answers.text: Tell the daughter the truth, as family have a right to know.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: They do not. This is private information, and sharing it without consent could cause serious harm to the person’s relationships and safety.

answers.text: Hint at it so the daughter can work it out for herself.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hinting still discloses private information the person shared in confidence. Keep it confidential unless she agrees you may share.

answers.text: Note it in the daily log for all staff to read.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Only share such information where it is genuinely necessary for care and the person agrees. Broadcasting it to all staff is not appropriate.

params.question: Which of these best helps create a welcoming, inclusive environment for LGBTQ+ people?

answers.text: Using inclusive language such as “partner” and making no assumptions about anyone’s identity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Inclusive language and an open, assumption-free approach help people feel safe to be themselves.

answers.text: Assuming everyone is heterosexual unless they say otherwise.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This assumption can make LGBTQ+ people feel invisible and unwelcome. Keep an open mind instead.

answers.text: Waiting for people to prove their identity before treating them respectfully.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Respect is never conditional. Everyone deserves inclusive, dignified care from the outset.

answers.text: Avoiding the subject entirely so no one is offended.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Silence can feel unwelcoming. Using inclusive language and being openly accepting is far more reassuring.
